data.title: India's GenAI course enrollments double in 2026 to 12 per min, says report
data.description:
India recorded 12 enrolments per minute in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) courses in 2026, double the rate of six per minute in 2025, according to a report by Coursera.
 
The Global Skills Report 2026 said India ranked 40th globally and 12th in the Asia Pacific region in its new AI-Human Skills Synergy Index, which assesses how learners across 98 countries are developing artificial intelligence and human skills together.
 
The report combines learning data from more than 300 million Coursera and Udemy learners with Oxford Insights’ Government AI Readiness Index 2025 to assess countries’ AI and human skills development, alongside government capacity, policy infrastructure and technology readiness.
 
 
AI micro-credential enrolments in India rose 181 per cent year-on-year, exceeding global growth of 122 per cent, while overall AI course enrolments increased 57 per cent. The report also found that demand was shifting towards more specialised applications, with enrolments in AI security growing 296 per cent and those in agentic workflows rising 238 per cent.
 

Human skills learning trails global growth

 
The report, however, found that growth in human skills learning in India was slower than global benchmarks, highlighting the need to strengthen capabilities such as critical thinking, problem-solving and innovation alongside AI proficiency.
 
Enrolments in critical thinking courses in India increased 65 per cent year-on-year, compared with global growth of 107 per cent. Complex problem-solving enrolments rose 55 per cent against 126 per cent globally, while innovation-related learning grew 62 per cent, compared with 74 per cent worldwide.
 
The report said these capabilities would be important for workers to question AI-generated outputs, challenge assumptions, solve problems and make sound decisions.
 
“India has the scale and ambition to become a global hub for AI talent, building capabilities that serve both our economy and the world,” said Ashutosh Gupta, managing director, India and APAC, Coursera.
 
“India leads the world in AI learning on Coursera. Building on this momentum means deepening specialist and domain-specific AI expertise while strengthening the human skills that give our workforce a competitive edge. Investing in both will be essential to turning AI adoption into productivity and growth,” he added.
 

AI learning becomes more specialised

 
The report also found that AI learning was becoming more applied and specialised. Apart from AI security and agentic workflows, GenAI enrolments grew 125 per cent year-on-year. Trending skill areas included AI and machine learning foundations, large language model applications and modelling, and prompting and AI interaction.
 
Learners were also combining AI capabilities with communication and innovation skills. The report identified pairings such as prompting and AI interaction with communication and presentation, and AI workflows, integration and orchestration with innovation and ideation.

data.title: HSBC reorganizes support roles in India, impacting hundreds of jobs
data.description:
By Rthvika Suvarna, Saikat Das and Ambereen Choudhury
 
HSBC Holdings Plc is consolidating some support functions in India as the Asia-focused lender steps up efforts to rein in costs and accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence. 
 
The bank recently told employees in India that it was centralizing finance functions across cities including Chennai, Gurugram and Bangalore and will no longer be housing those roles in other hubs, including Hyderabad and Pune, according to people with knowledge of the matter, who requested not to be named because the information is private.
 
The changes are confined to finance roles within HSBC’s so-called global capability centers in India, and employees expect the move to affect several hundred roles, according to the people. HSBC staff will be given the option and support to relocate, but the bank won’t provide further cash incentives for them to move, the people added.
  
HSBC has been weighing deep job cuts over the coming years as Chief Executive Officer Georges Elhedery deploys AI to shrink its middle and back offices. Non-client facing roles in global service centers are among those expected to be most impacted, people familiar have said previously. The changes could ultimately impact around 20,000 roles — or about 10% of its total workforce.
 
“As we simplify the bank, our focus remains on ensuring we have the right roles in the right locations to support the best customer outcomes,” an HSBC spokesperson said in a statement, referring to the roles in India. “We are taking the best of our people experience and combining this with emerging technologies to deliver outcomes that are better, faster, and safer for our clients.”
 
India has emerged as a key market for HSBC, alongside other major banks. HSBC describes itself as the largest foreign lender in the country and generated $1.9 billion of pretax profit in the region in 2025. It had about 47,000 employees in India at the end of last year. About 42,500 employees work in the global capability centers in India, including on technology, according to estimates from a person familiar with the matter.
 
Other banks have also been reshaping their Indian hubs, which have grown so large that Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and JPMorgan now employ more people in India than anywhere else outside the US. They are using AI to automate work such as checking loan documents, reconciling accounts and writing basic code, the same tasks that once gave fresh graduates their first jobs at those centers. 
 
Lenders globally are expecting AI to lead to fewer roles in the future. Standard Chartered Plc plans to cut close to 8,000 support roles over four years, while JPMorgan Chase & Co. CEO Jamie Dimon has said the technology will eliminate jobs broadly across industries. Banks are trimming junior analyst classes by as much as two-thirds, Debasish Patnaik, a senior partner at McKinsey & Co., said in June.
 
At HSBC, Elhedery has accelerated an overhaul of Europe’s largest bank through asset sales and operational simplification. 
 
In August, the lender said it expects its global restructuring effort to yield $2 billion in cost savings, up from an earlier target of $1.5 billion. The banker has made streamlining HSBC a central principle, saying earlier this year that he had been “ruthless about killing complexity” at the lender.

data.title: Uttar Pradesh Civil Aviation Promotion Policy, 2017: Incentives, connectivity and implementation
data.description:
POLICY AT A GLANCE

ItemPosition
Official titleCivil Aviation Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh, 2017
Government order dateAugust 25, 2017
Administrative departmentCivil Aviation Department, Uttar Pradesh
Implementing authority for aviation incentivesDirector, Civil Aviation, Government of Uttar Pradesh
Main focusRegional air connectivity, airport infrastructure, airline incentives, air cargo, MRO and aviation skills
RCS fuel-tax supportVAT on aviation turbine fuel reduced/waived to the policy-prescribed level for ten years on eligible RCS flights
State share of RCS viability-gap funding20 per cent
Seat underwritingRs 2,500 per eligible vacant seat under prescribed conditions
RCS ticket-tax support100 per cent reimbursement of eligible State GST on air tickets, initially for three years
Airport parking/night haltZero charges at state-owned RCS airports, initially for three years
Airline office spaceUp to 100 sq m at zero rent at state-owned no-frills RCS airports, initially for three years
RNFC reimbursement50 per cent, up to Rs 2,000, for eligible RCS/divisional-headquarter routes
MRO incentive100 per cent State GST reimbursement on eligible MRO job contracts and 50 per cent reimbursement on eligible aircraft parts/accessories for ten years
Current statusStill officially listed, although many route-specific incentives were expressly time-bound and later aviation policies address MRO and airstrip development separately

 What is the Civil Aviation Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh, 2017?

The Civil Aviation Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh, 2017, was Uttar Pradesh's first comprehensive civil aviation policy. Its central purpose was not simply to build airports, but to make new regional routes commercially viable, upgrade underused airstrips and create an aviation ecosystem covering passenger services, cargo, maintenance, training and airport infrastructure.

 

The policy was framed alongside the Government of India's National Civil Aviation Policy, 2016 and Regional Connectivity Scheme, or RCS-UDAN.

At the time, Uttar Pradesh had a relatively small number of airports with scheduled services, while several state-owned airstrips and defence airports had either limited civil use or no scheduled connectivity. The policy therefore sought to combine Union government RCS support with additional state incentives.

It also supported the planned greenfield airport at Jewar, now Noida International Airport, through the broader strategy of airport infrastructure development.

 Why was the policy introduced?

UP had no comprehensive civil aviation policy before 2017 and that the first round of RCS bidding had not produced adequate connectivity for the state. The government therefore set out to:

  • Improve air connectivity through new RCS routes
  • Connect underserved and unserved airstrips
  • Improve links among non-RCS airports
  • Use aviation to support tourism
  • Facilitate trade and employment
  • Promote air cargo for agricultural exports, perishables, manufacturing and e-commerce
  • Develop trained aviation professionals
  • Encourage MRO facilities
  • Attract investment in airport and aviation-support infrastructure

The policy's baseline data are historical. For example, it cited passenger traffic of about 6.1 million in 2016-17 and identified only a small set of airports with meaningful scheduled operations at the time. Those figures should not be read as describing the state's present aviation network.

 How did the policy support airport development?

The policy envisaged development of both greenfield and brownfield airports. For brownfield airports, land-acquisition or procurement costs could be borne by the Airports Authority of India, the state government or shared between them on mutually agreed terms.

Investment in new airports, airport upgrades, airstrips, heliports, helipads and associated air-transport infrastructure may qualify for incentives under the Uttar Pradesh Industrial Investment and Employment Promotion Policy, 2017, subject to the applicable eligibility conditions.

The policy also envisaged upgrading airstrips into no-frills airports, particularly where RCS routes were awarded. It stated that the Airports Authority of India could develop such airports with Government of India assistance, while Uttar Pradesh could form a special-purpose vehicle with AAI, develop airports through a state company or explore public-private partnership structures.

 What support was offered for aircraft manufacturing?

The 2017 policy included an early manufacturing incentive.

For aircraft or helicopters manufactured or assembled in Uttar Pradesh, the policy provided reimbursement of the corresponding State Goods and Services Tax receivable by the state for ten years, subject to a maximum of ten aircraft or helicopters.

Where an airline purchased an aircraft or helicopter manufactured or assembled in Uttar Pradesh and deployed it primarily on Uttar Pradesh routes for at least five years, the acquisition could also qualify for eligible incentives under the Industrial Investment and Employment Promotion Policy, 2017.

For this purpose, a route was considered primarily connected with Uttar Pradesh where at least half of the aircraft's take-offs were from airports in the state.

These provisions should be distinguished from later defence, aerospace and aircraft-MRO policies, which introduced more specialised incentive structures.

 What aviation-support infrastructure was covered?

The policy also extended eligible industrial incentives to aviation-support infrastructure, including aircraft maintenance, ground handling, air cargo, warehousing and passenger transport facilities at airports.

Eligible projects could access capital-interest or infrastructure-interest assistance available under the then Industrial Investment and Employment Promotion Policy.

The civil aviation policy did not itself set a single universal subsidy percentage for every such investment. Instead, it linked qualifying infrastructure to the applicable industrial-policy provisions.

 How did the policy support air cargo?

Air cargo was identified as an important tool for improving agricultural exports, movement of perishables, manufacturing supply chains and e-commerce.

The policy supported the development of air-cargo and logistics infrastructure by offering incentives for air cargo hubs and related facilities, facilitating fulfilment centres and single-window support for cargo and logistics businesses, and promoting airport infrastructure for handling perishable goods.

The government's intention was therefore broader than passenger connectivity. Airports were also to function as logistics nodes capable of handling high-value and time-sensitive goods.

 What MRO incentives were available?

The policy gave specific fiscal support to Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul facilities. For eligible MRO operations, it provided:

  • 100 per cent reimbursement of State GST levied on MRO job contracts from domestic or international airlines
  • 50 per cent reimbursement of State GST levied on the purchase of aircraft parts and accessories used for maintenance
  • Both incentives for 10 years

It also allowed eligible investment incentives under the 2017 industrial policy for expenditure on hangars and other necessary MRO infrastructure.

The policy specifically identified the area around the proposed Jewar airport as having potential for an MRO hub.

Uttar Pradesh later introduced a standalone Aircraft Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul Policy in 2022. Fresh MRO investment should therefore be evaluated under the later MRO framework rather than assuming that the 2017 provisions remain the primary scheme.

 How did the policy support aviation skills?

The policy recognised that the expansion of airports and airlines would require a skilled workforce, including pilots, aircraft maintenance engineers, ground-handling personnel, cabin crew, IT professionals and other airport-support staff. It proposed promoting aviation-related courses at technical institutes and universities in UP.

It also stated that existing scholarship arrangements for diploma and graduate courses would be extended to eligible courses related to aircraft maintenance engineering, cabin crew and other aviation professions. A dedicated cell at the directorate level was proposed to engage airlines and help with placement of aviation professionals.

These were ecosystem-development provisions rather than a universal cash subsidy payable directly to every aviation trainee.

 What incentives were provided for non-RCS routes?

The policy also attempted to create new links involving airports that were not covered by RCS. At the time, Lucknow, Gorakhpur and Varanasi were identified as non-RCS airports. Incentives for new connections involving non-RCS airports were initially valid for one year, and generally applied to a single flight per route awarded to the first eligible proposer.

For qualifying new flights connecting a non-RCS airport in UP with another non-RCS airport inside or outside the state, the policy provided:

  • Waiver of VAT on aviation turbine fuel for one year
  • Reimbursement of State GST received by the state on ticket sales for one year

 Additional support for intra-state links

For specified routes connecting Lucknow, Varanasi and Gorakhpur, the policy also provided:

  • Compensation equivalent to the state's viability-gap-funding share of Rs 400 per seat on 50 per cent of eligible seats, subject to the prescribed limit;
  • Seat underwriting at Rs 2,500 per vacant seat, covering 15 per cent of total seats and capped at 360 seats per month per one-way trip.

These were temporary route-development incentives and should not be presented as permanently available benefits in 2026.

 What is RCS-UDAN?

The Regional Connectivity Scheme, or UDAN, was introduced by the Government of India to connect unserved and underserved airports at affordable fares.

Under the 2017 policy, an underserved airport was one with no more than seven scheduled commercial departures a week. An unserved airport was one with no scheduled flights during the preceding two approved flight schedules.

The policy adopted definitions under the Union RCS framework and stated that later changes in the central scheme would automatically apply unless the state policy provided otherwise.

 What support did Uttar Pradesh provide under RCS?

The state committed to several forms of mandatory and additional support.

Aviation turbine fuel tax

The policy provided for VAT on aviation turbine fuel at the RCS-prescribed concessional level. Its fiscal-incentive section states that VAT would be waived for ten years on eligible RCS flights beginning after April 1, 2017, while the underlying RCS memorandum referred to reducing VAT to 1 per cent.

The Invest UP summary currently presents the headline incentive as zero VAT on ATF for ten years at RCS airports.

Because tax treatment can be affected by subsequent notifications, the operative tax order for the relevant period should govern any actual claim.

Viability-gap funding

The state agreed to bear 20 per cent of the viability-gap funding payable for eligible RCS routes.

Viability-gap funding compensates airlines for operating eligible regional routes that may not initially generate sufficient commercial revenue.

Land and airport services

The state agreed to provide, where required:

  • Minimum land free of cost and free from encumbrances for RCS airport development
  • Security services
  • Fire services
  • Concessional electricity
  • Water
  • Road and multimodal connectivity
  • Facilitation of aviation-fuel infrastructure

At state-owned RCS airports, land for oil marketing companies to establish aviation turbine fuel infrastructure could be provided at zero rent.

 How did seat underwriting work?

Seat underwriting was an additional state incentive intended to reduce an airline's revenue risk.

For small Category-1 aircraft with up to 20 seats directly connecting Lucknow with divisional headquarters, the state could underwrite 100 per cent of non-VGF seats, subject to a maximum of 300 seats per month per one-way trip.

For larger Category-2 and Category-3 aircraft or other eligible RCS routes, 30 per cent of non-VGF seats could be underwritten, subject to a maximum of 360 seats per month per one-way trip.

The underwriting rate was Rs 2,500 per eligible vacant seat, initially for three years.

Airlines were expected first to attempt to sell the seats commercially. Unsold seats could then be made available to the state shortly before departure. Government officials could use allocated seats without additional payment, while eligible seats remaining vacant could be reimbursed under the underwriting mechanism.

 What other airline incentives were available?

For eligible RCS operations, the policy provided several additional concessions:

IncentivePolicy provision
State GST on RCS air tickets100 per cent reimbursement, initially for 3 years
Aircraft parking/night haltZero charge at state-owned RCS airports, initially for 3 years
Airline office spaceUp to 100 sq m at zero rent at state-owned no-frills airports, initially for 3 years
Route Navigation and Facilitation Charges50 per cent reimbursement up to Rs 2,000, initially for 3 years
ElectricitySubsidy of Rs 4 per unit up to 30,000 units per month at eligible RCS airports
WaterProvided free by the state
Fire servicesProvided free by the state
Road connectivityTo be provided and maintained by the Public Works Department
Bus serviceTo be provided through the Uttar Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation

These concessions were route- and airport-specific and, in several cases, explicitly limited to an initial three-year period.

 Which airports and airstrips were targeted?

The policy identified numerous existing, underserved and unserved airports or airstrips as potential RCS locations.

Its initial development strategy included airstrips at:

  • Meerut
  • Moradabad
  • Ayodha
  • Saharanpur
  • Jhansi
  • Chitrakoot
  • Azamgarh
  • Aligarh
  • Sonbhadra
  • Shravasti

The policy also identified airport connectivity as a tool for tourism, including destinations such as Agra, Varanasi, Kushinagar, Ayodhya, Chitrakoot and Dudhwa.

These lists represented the development priorities of 2017 and should not be used as a current statement of airport status.

 How was the policy implemented?

The Director, Civil Aviation, Government of Uttar Pradesh was designated as the implementing agency for fiscal incentives under the policy. A separate nodal officer was to be appointed for allocation of non-VGF seats to state government travellers.

Airlines and operators were required to meet Directorate General of Civil Aviation standards. Receiving a state incentive did not replace licensing, airworthiness, route or safety requirements imposed by national aviation regulators.

 Implementation and current status

The expansion in Uttar Pradesh's aviation network since 2017 has been substantial.

Invest UP currently reports 15 functional airports, compared with four functional airports in 2017, and says these connect more than 80 destinations. It identifies Lucknow, Varanasi, Gorakhpur, Agra, Prayagraj, Bareilly, Kanpur, Hindon, Kushinagar, Ayodhya, Aligarh, Azamgarh, Shravasti, Chitrakoot and Moradabad as functional.

The same official source reports that domestic passenger traffic increased from 87.90 lakh in financial year 2019-20 to 102.08 lakh in FY24, while cargo traffic rose from 18,615 tonnes to 25,915 tonnes over the same period.

The Uttar Pradesh Budget 2026-27 proposes Rs 2,111 crore for civil aviation, including Rs 750 crore for Jewar International Airport and Rs 1,100 crore for construction, expansion, strengthening and land acquisition for state airstrips.

The 2017 policy remains officially listed by Invest UP alongside the separate Aircraft MRO Policy, 2022 and Airstrip Policy, 2023.

That does not mean every original incentive remains open-ended. Many airline incentives in the 2017 policy were expressly limited to one or three years after commencement of an eligible route.

 Key challenges and practical considerations

  • Route viability: Regional routes may still become unsustainable once temporary subsidies expire.
  • Airline participation: Airport infrastructure alone cannot guarantee scheduled services.
  • Demand concentration: Traffic remains concentrated around larger economic and tourism centres.
  • Airport economics: Smaller airports face fixed operating costs even at low passenger volumes.
  • Regulatory dependence: Aviation safety, route approvals and airline licensing remain Union subjects.
  • Policy layering: Investors must now distinguish the 2017 framework from later MRO, airstrip and industrial policies.
  • Attribution: Growth in airports or passenger traffic cannot be assigned solely to one state policy.

 FAQs

What was the main objective of the policy?

To expand regional air connectivity and aviation infrastructure while supporting tourism, trade, cargo, MRO and aviation employment.

What was the state share of RCS viability-gap funding?

Uttar Pradesh committed to 20 per cent of eligible VGF under the RCS framework.

What was the seat-underwriting rate?

Rs 2,500 per qualifying vacant seat, subject to route, aircraft and monthly limits.

Did airlines receive tax support?

Yes. Eligible RCS routes received aviation-fuel tax concessions and reimbursement of State GST on air-ticket sales under the prescribed conditions.

Was MRO supported?

Yes. The policy provided ten-year State GST reimbursement incentives for eligible MRO job contracts and aircraft parts. A separate MRO policy was later introduced in 2022.

Is the policy still relevant?

Yes, it remains officially listed, but several airline and route incentives were time-bound and later policies now govern specialised areas such as MRO and state airstrips.

 Conclusion

The Civil Aviation Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh, 2017 marked the state's shift from airport infrastructure development alone towards an integrated regional-connectivity strategy.

Its most distinctive measures were aviation-fuel tax concessions, a 20 per cent state contribution to RCS viability-gap funding, seat underwriting, reimbursement of ticket-related State GST, free or subsidised airport services and support for MRO, air cargo and aviation skills.

Uttar Pradesh's airport network has expanded significantly since 2017, but that growth reflects a combination of state policy, Union government RCS support, airport investment and market demand. The 2017 policy should therefore be assessed principally as an enabling framework that helped establish the state's regional aviation strategy, rather than as the sole cause of subsequent airport and traffic growth.

 Sources

  • Civil Aviation Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh, 2017, Civil Aviation Department, Government of Uttar Pradesh.
  • Uttar Pradesh Civil Aviation Promotion Policy 2017, Invest UP, Government of Uttar Pradesh.
  • Civil Aviation Sector, Invest UP, Government of Uttar Pradesh.
  • Civil Aviation Promotion Policy of Uttar Pradesh - 2017, Nivesh Mitra, Government of Uttar Pradesh.
  • Uttar Pradesh Budget 2026-27, Finance Department, Government of Uttar Pradesh.

data.title: China industrial profit growth hits 5-month high as recovery remains uneven
data.description:
Profit growth at China's industrial firms accelerated in October to the fastest in five months, supported by improving conditions in parts of the manufacturing sector, although broader economic momentum remained subdued.
 
The industrial profits data are closely watched as a gauge of corporate health, investment appetite and the effectiveness of Beijing's stimulus measures. The figures also offer clues on whether stronger earnings could reduce pressure for further policy easing.
 
Profits at industrial ‌firms rose 20.1% from a year earlier last month, versus  a 14.4% gain in September, data from  the National Bureau of Statistics showed on Friday. Profits were up 16% in the first 10 months, accelerating from a  15.5% increase in the January-September period.
 
 
But the breakdown highlighted a widening divergence across sectors.
 
Profit growth in AI-related industries and upstream sectors is outpacing that of downstream industries, while external demand remains an important source of support, said Ding Meng, CITIC Bank International's chief China economist.
 
The bureau's data showed that profits in computer, telecommunications and other electronic equipment manufacturing doubled in the first 10 months,  while furniture manufacturing posted a decline of 52.4%.
 
"The recovery remains uneven and provides a more mixed signal on the health of the broader ‌economy," said Lynn Song, ING's Greater China chief economist.
 
Broader Chinese indices were muted while tech stocks rebounded strongly. The  CSI Semiconductor Industry Index jumped more than 5%, while the Hang Seng Tech Index was up 3%.
 
The disparity underscores the challenges facing policymakers as domestic demand remains weak and continues to weigh on large parts of the corporate sector. Many manufacturers have increasingly relied on overseas sales ‌to sustain growth, leaving them exposed to rising trade  frictions and geopolitical risks.
 
Beijing has rolled out a ‌series of support measures in recent months, including interest-rate cuts, liquidity injections and targeted financing support for sectors such as technology, ‌manufacturing and infrastructure.
 
Still, analysts say the impact has been mixed, with weak household demand and lingering strains in the property  sector continuing to drag on the broader recovery.
 
"The robust pace of profit growth further reinforces expectations that there will be no additional monetary policy easing in the near term," Ding said.
 
The outlook  for exports, a key source of support for manufacturers this year, has also become less certain. Concern over potential tariff increases and other trade restrictions, particularly in the United States and the European Union, has raised ‌questions about the sustainability of export-driven growth.
 
Looking ahead, a potential slowdown in AI data centre investment, concerns over AI-sector profitability and ‌leverage, and the risk of further Western restrictions on Chinese exports mean that "boosting domestic demand as soon as possible remains the key to sustaining profit growth," Ding said.
 
Industrial profit figures cover firms with annual revenue of at least 20 million yuan ($3 million) from main operations.

data.title: Zydus Life shares dip 3% on USFDA's CRL to new drug; MOFSL stays 'neutral'
data.description:
Zydus Lifesciences share price: Shares of Zydus Lifesciences declined nearly 3 per cent in Friday's intraday trading session after the US Food and Drug Administration (USFDA) issued a Complete Response Letter (CRL) to the New Drug Application (NDA) for Saroglitazar, likely delaying its launch.
 
The CRL relates to the company’s ongoing review of the resolution plan addressing observations from the October 2026 inspection of the Moraiya facility, rather than the drug’s clinical data.
 
Following this announcement, Zydus Lifesciences' share price hit the day's low of ₹1,157.15 on the BSE, down 2.96 per cent from its last closing price of ₹1,192.50.
 
As of 9.27 am, the scrip was trading off its day's low, but down 0.7 per cent at ₹1,184.25. At the same time, BSE Sensex was down 0.44 per cent at 83,985.
 
 
The pharma stock has seen a sharp rise this year, gaining 30 per cent on a year-to-date (YTD) basis, while it remains 85 per cent higher over three years, BSE data shows. 
ALSO READ: Stock Market LIVE: Sensex down 200 pts, Nifty tests 25,800; SMIDs outperform
 
Commenting on the USFDA's CRL to Saroglitazar, domestic brokerage Motilal Oswal Financial Services (MOFSL) said that its analysis on inspection classification indicates three scenarios in terms of timing of product approval from the USFDA, with the earliest being June-July 2027 or the latest being 1-2 years.
 
For Zydus, Saroglitazar Magnesium is the promising product for the US market in the primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) indication and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) indication, said MOFSL in a note.
 
Despite entering as the third product, Zydus is targeting ~20 per cent patient share over the long term, with an initial ambition of 10-12 per cent by FY30. Management clarified that it was not seeking parity with existing therapies but intended to establish a differentiated position through its clinical and safety profile.
 
MOFSL analysts said they expect earnings to compound at 6 per cent over FY26-28, with a decline in FY27 to be followed by a healthy recovery in FY28. FY27 is likely to be a year of high operating costs as the company invests in its specialty portfolio, with benefits expected to accrue from FY28 onward, subject to timely regulatory approvals. A more meaningful ramp-up is envisaged during FY29-F30, it noted.
 
Given the limited upside from the current level, the brokerage said it maintains a 'Neutral' stance on the stock with a target price of ₹1,280.

data.title: Urban Company gains 2% on AC biz entry; Voltas, Blue Star, Havells fall
data.description:
Shares of Home-services platform Urban Company gained nearly 2 per cent in early trade on Friday after the company announced its foray into the air conditioner category through its brand Native Ultra and Native Ultra Air ACs
 
The company’s counter at 09:18 AM was trading 0.7 per cent higher at ₹171 per share on NSE. In comparison, Nifty 50 was down 0.08 per cent at 25,605.35. In intraday trade, the stock gained 1.7 per cent to touch the day's high at ₹172.96 per share.
 
Urban Company said that Native AC comes with a five-year unconditional warranty that covers gas refills, meaning zero repair costs for five years, along with a 10-year compressor warranty. The company further added that over the years it has handled more than 18 million AC service and repair jobs. 
 
 
Native AC, priced at ₹55,499 onwards, were made available for pre-booking from November 26, 2026, exclusively on the Urban Company app, with assisted buying available. The full range will be announced at launch.
 
Brokerage firm SBI Securities has given the company a positive rating ‘in the medium to long term’
 
Vipin Kumar, AVP research at Globe Capital Market, said that the stock has started a series of higher highs and higher lows after hitting an all-time low around ₹100 on March 4, 2026. Going ahead, we advise traders to maintain a buy-on-dips approach and wait for a dip to add around the ₹155–₹160 levels. “On the higher side, 185 will act as immediate resistance. A decisive break above ₹185 could lead it towards its all-time highs,” he added. 
 
The company’s listed peers include Voltas, which is a likely market leader in the AC segment, followed by LG Electronics India, Blue Star, Havells through the Lloyd brand, and Johnson Controls-Hitachi
 
Notably, on Friday Voltas’ share price dipped over 3 per cent to hit an intraday low of ₹1,211 apiece, followed by a 2 per cent dip in Blue Star share price at ₹1,743 per share. Meanwhile, Havells’ share price also fell 1.4 per cent intraday.

data.title: Rupee plunges 24 paise to 92.62 against US dollar during early trade
data.description:
The rupee plunged 24 paise to 92.62 against the US dollar in early trade on Friday, dragged down by a recovery in crude oil prices and subdued sentiment in domestic equity markets.

Sustained inflow of foreign funds and a softening dollar capped the fall in the Indian currency, forex traders said.

In the interbank foreign exchange market, the rupee opened at 92.44 and declined to 92.62 against the greenback, trading 24 paise lower from its previous close.

On Thursday, the rupee settled down 18 paise to 92.38 against the US dollar, a day after jumping 65 paise to reach its highest level this fiscal year so far.

 

The Indian currency became the best-performing Asian currency, recovering nearly 5 per cent from its lowest-ever close of 96.88 against the US dollar recorded on October 8.

Meanwhile, the dollar index, which gauges the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, was at 103.65, lower by 0.07 per cent.

Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, was trading 0.11 per cent lower at USD 96.46 per barrel in futures trade.

Analysts said that oil prices breached the USD 95-a-barrel level after reports of vessels being targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, fuelling concerns over supply-chain disruptions.

In the domestic equity market, Sensex fell 350.25 points or 0.42 per cent to 83,978.34, while the Nifty was down 79.05 points or 0.31 per cent to 25,807.25.

Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) bought equities worth Rs 5,843.33 crore on a net basis on Thursday, according to exchange data.

data.title: Nifty IT index flags breakout from 3 important chart patterns; details here
data.description:
Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited. They do not reflect the views of Business Standard. Readers are advised to exercise discretion. Brokerages PL Capital and Emkay in their technical reports on the Nifty IT highlighted that the index has broken out from three important chart patterns on the daily charts. The Nifty IT index has moved up 2.4 per cent to 33,387 thus far in November. However, it has rallied 20.5 per cent thus far in the last quarter of 2026, and up almost 30 per cent from its nadir this year. The IT index has witnessed a sharp reversal since July. Prior to this, the index was the top laggard this year, down nearly 29 per cent in the January - June period. Following the recovery, brokerages believe the Nifty IT index now looks favourably placed on the charts and could see a trend reversal here on. CHECK Stock Market LIVE Updates 

PL Capital flags breakout from 'Golden Cross' and 'Descending Trendline'

Further a descending trendline is formed joining the preceding highs (lower highs) on the charts. The Nifty IT has witnessed a strong recovery and is currently testing its long-term descending trendline resistance at 33,000–33,300, says PL Capital. "The formation of a Golden Cross, coupled with a rising RSI at 63.42 and early signs of improvement in Relative Strength (RS) against Nifty 50, indicates a strengthening technical structure," explains the brokerage. Analysts at PL Capital reckon that a decisive weekly close above the trendline, supported by higher volumes, could pave the way for a move towards 35,500 and subsequently 38,000–39,000, thus marking a potential reversal of the prolonged corrective phase for the IT index. The brokerage adds that the 30,100–30,600 zone remains a key support area. Check - TOP GAINERS NSE | TOP LOSERS NSE

data.title: Tata Steel-Apollo deal tests India's reinforced corporate governance rules
data.description:
By Anto Antony and Samie Modak
 
A deal that would hand Tata Steel Ltd. control of a smaller rival triggered a dramatic show of investor anger this week, turning the plan into a test of India’s reinforced corporate governance rules.
 
The basics of the agreement are messy. Tata Steel, a $22 billion piece of the sprawling Tata conglomerate, plans to take a 26.6% share in APL Apollo Tubes Ltd., buying out founder Sanjay Gupta and triggering a mandatory offer for a further 26%. APL Apollo will in turn take Tata’s tubes and color-coated steel business, a deal it will fund initially with debt. Gupta, meanwhile, stays in the business with his family’s SG Tech Engineering agreeing to provide color-coated steel to the new owners.
 
 
For Tata, the purchase is a way of growing in higher-margin corners of the steel market. In the eyes of angry shareholders — who wiped more than $4 billion off the companies’ combined market value over two trading days — it’s a worryingly costly plan, and one that allows Gupta to exit with cash while the remaining APL Apollo investors are left to shoulder an unclear amount of debt, dilution and risk. 
 
The fight is raising questions about India’s ability to enforce minority shareholder protections and ensure that wealth created by tycoons can trickle down.
 
“The real test of India’s corporate governance reforms is whether they can protect minority shareholders when their interests diverge from those of the country’s most powerful business groups,” said Shriram Subramanian, founder and managing director of proxy advisory firm InGovern Research Services.
 
The backlash has already prompted Tata Steel to consider changes to the offer, leaving investors to watch for its next steps.
 
“It would send a clear message that strategic rationale alone is not sufficient to secure shareholder support,” said Akhilesh Kumar, research analyst at Emkay Global Financial Services. “Companies need to ensure that the transaction structure, valuation and funding arrangements are acceptable to all stakeholders, particularly minority shareholders.”
 
A Tata Steel spokesperson said the company was “carefully examining the concerns to determine how best to address them.” Apollo’s Gupta did not immediately respond to Bloomberg queries. 
 
Founding families have been and remain central to India’s economic transformation, building sprawling business empires spanning telecommunications, financial services, energy and infrastructure. Many retain significant control of listed companies even as foreign institutional investors and domestic savers increasingly finance their expansion.
 
Even after a dramatic expansion of India’s stock market over the past decade, founders owned just under 42% of non-state-owned Indian companies at the end of September, while institutional investors held less than 35%, according to corporate information database primeinfobase.com.
 
To counter that weight and to avoid a repeat of major accounting scandals — including the 2009 debacle at Satyam Computer Services Ltd., once one of the country’s largest software exporters — India has tightened oversight and governance rules over the past decade or so.
 
The securities regulator has also strengthened minority shareholders’ powers to block major transactions involving corporate insiders. Rules that took effect in April 2023 extended those safeguards to transactions with unrelated entities if their purpose and effect are to benefit related parties.
 
As a result, there have been notable successes. For example, investors blocked tycoon Anil Agarwal’s 2020 attempt to take Vedanta Ltd. private at what they considered to be a cut-price valuation. Life Insurance Corp. of India, one of the company’s largest public shareholders, said publicly that it would not tender stock below 320 rupees a share — almost four times Vedanta’s indicative price — and investors held out for better terms. The delisting ultimately failed.
 
Earlier this year, rules protecting minority investors allowed shareholders at Linde India Ltd. to reject a proposed transaction with Praxair India, controlled by the same majority owner.
 
Still, there are also incidents where so-called promoters won the day — from some vocal shareholders’ efforts to stop the delisting of ICICI Bank’s brokerage arm last year, to fund manager Invesco’s earlier failure to oust the chief executive of Zee Entertainment.
 
The Tata deal is a test with repercussions at a time when India’s stock market wants to retain domestic and foreign investors eager to bet on its economic growth, even at valuations that sit well above that of other emerging economies.
 
“India’s economic growth alone cannot sustain the valuation premium its companies command in global markets,” said K.G. Suresh, a faculty member at the Indian Institute of Management Bodh Gaya. “Any erosion of investor confidence in corporate governance risks raising the cost of capital for Indian businesses.”
 
The controversy comes at an awkward time for the Tata Group. Its privately held holding company, Tata Sons Pvt., has been embroiled in a months-long dispute over leadership, governance and a regulator-mandated stock market listing.
 
“While the Tata Group is known for its impeccable governance and shareholder friendly conduct, this time around it seems to have been caught in a bind,” said Ankit Agrawal, chief investment officer at Yellowstone Equity, an independent research firm. “It seems Tata Steel got carried away by the hefty valuation being accorded to their color-coated sheets business and the desperation to expand their downstream business.”
 
India’s market watchdog is examining the structure of the transaction, according to people familiar with the matter. A representative of the Securities and Exchange Board of India did not respond to a request for comment.

data.title: TVS family feud: What rights do daughters have over family business assets?
data.description:
Lakshmi Venu approached the Madras High Court on Wednesday, seeking partition of the joint family assets of the Venu Srinivasan branch of the TVS family. The move has brought the question of daughters’ inheritance rights in family-run businesses into focus.
 
The dispute concerns an arrangement reached within the family in 2024. While Venu Srinivasan maintains that the division was fair to both his children, Lakshmi and her mother, Mallika Srinivasan, are of the view that the division of business responsibilities did not settle their economic interests in the family assets.
 
The ownership structure adds another layer of complexity to the dispute. Interests in businesses such as TVS Holdings, TVS Motor Company, TVS Credit Services and Sundaram-Clayton are held through the VS Trust and other holding entities. The question now is whether the arrangements governing the allocation of assets within the family branch are legally valid.
 

Can daughters claim a share in family wealth during their father’s lifetime?

Yes, daughters can claim a share in the family’s wealth, depending on the nature of the property.
 
Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, recognises a daughter as a coparcener in a Hindu Mitakshara joint family. This means she acquires an equal right by birth in coparcenary property, just like a son. She can seek partition and is also subject to the same liabilities in respect of that property.
 
Coparcenary property refers to ancestral or joint family property held collectively by coparceners within a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF), in which eligible family members acquire a legal right by birth.
 
The Supreme Court, in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma, clarified that a daughter’s coparcenary rights do not depend on whether her father was alive when the amendment took effect. The right is acquired by birth, provided the coparcenary existed when the amendment came into force.

How does the law distinguish between ancestral and self-acquired business assets?

The distinction is based on the source of funding, lineage and whether the assets have been partitioned or merged with joint family property. The distinction is relevant under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
 
Ancestral or coparcenary property includes property inherited by a Hindu from ancestors under conditions recognised by Mitakshara law. Self-acquired property, on the other hand, includes assets purchased or developed by an individual using personal funds.
 
A father has the right to dispose of his self-acquired property at his discretion during his lifetime.
 
“The Supreme Court has consistently held that the mere existence of a joint Hindu family does not raise a presumption that its properties are joint family properties,” said Rishabh Gandhi, former judge and founder, Rishabh Gandhi and Advocates.
 
Property inherited under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, does not ordinarily become coparcenary property in the hands of the heir, Gandhi added.

Can business assets held through family trusts be claimed in a partition suit?

Under Indian law, business assets held through a family trust generally cannot be directly partitioned in an ordinary partition suit, given the distinction between legal ownership and beneficial interests. Section 3 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, defines a trust as an obligation attached to the ownership of property.
 
“Private trusts are governed by the Indian Trusts Act, 1882. Its beneficiary rights include compelling the trustee to perform his duties and restraining a threatened breach of trust,” said Ray Vikram Nath, senior partner, Aretha Alpha.
 
Nath added that challenging the settlement of joint family property on the grounds that the settlor had no authority to alienate it rests on general principles of trust law rather than a specific judicial precedent cited in support of the argument. Such a legal challenge would be difficult to sustain, he said.

Is dividing management control the same as dividing ownership of family wealth?

No. Management and ownership are legally distinct concepts.
 
For instance, a family may decide that one child will manage a manufacturing business while another will look after a different business. Such an arrangement determines who runs the enterprise, but it does not establish ownership of the underlying assets or shares.
 
This distinction is important in the context of the March 2024 memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed by Venu Srinivasan, Mallika Srinivasan, Lakshmi and Sudarshan Venu. The arrangement is now a matter of dispute.
 
“Assigning operational control of different verticals to individual family members may settle day-to-day governance, but it does not by itself transfer underlying or beneficial value,” said Nitin Jain, partner, Agama Law Associates.
 
For a division of ownership to be durable, the transfer of economic interests must be formally documented and executed. An informal operational arrangement without corresponding ownership transfers remains vulnerable to challenge, Jain added.

Can an earlier family settlement prevent a daughter from seeking partition?

A valid family settlement is binding on its parties and prevents them from reopening matters that have already been resolved.
 
The Supreme Court, in Kale v. Deputy Director of Consolidation (1976), recognised the legal validity of bona fide family arrangements intended to resolve disputes and preserve harmony within the family.
 
“A daughter who signed can still challenge it for fraud, coercion, suppression of facts, or because it never actually settled her ownership. That is hard if she signed and took benefits, as estoppel then applies,” Nath added.

Can a family partition suit alter ownership and control of listed companies?

A partition suit does not transfer the assets of a listed company to individual family members.
 
Under company law, a company is a separate legal entity. Its assets belong to the company, while shareholders own shares that confer rights under the Companies Act, 2013, and the company’s articles.
 
The outcome of the TVS dispute will depend on the character of the assets, the trust arrangements and the validity of earlier settlements. “The court will now have to examine the earlier family agreements, the nature of the assets and whether Lakshmi's economic rights were actually settled,” said Alay Razvi, managing partner, Accord Juris.
 
“From a legal standpoint, the matter highlights the interplay between statutory inheritance rights, family settlement arrangements and the nature of asset ownership, particularly in multigenerational business families,” said Ankit Rajgarhia, partner, Bahuguna Law Associates.
